Chapter 8: The Interplay of Principles—Designing for Virality
Now that we've explored all six principles—social currency, triggers, emotion, public visibility, practical value, and stories—it’s pretty clear that truly contagious ideas don’t just lean on one of them. Instead, the most viral concepts actually combine these principles in ways that amplify their power. It’s the way these elements work together that really sparks virality.
Think of this framework like a set of gears, each one connected to the next. When you turn one gear, you set the others in motion. For instance, picture a story that stirs up strong emotions and is genuinely useful. If that story’s also linked to something people see or do often—and it’s easy for others to spot—suddenly, you’ve got something people can’t help but share. The more principles you tap into, the stronger the momentum gets.
Let’s make this real with an example. Imagine a charity campaign that asks people to post photos of themselves doing acts of kindness. This campaign brings several principles together:
Social currency—people feel good about sharing their good deeds. Triggers—the campaign is tied to a certain day each week, making it easy to remember. Emotion—acts of kindness inspire positive feelings. Public visibility—photos are posted on social media for everyone to see. Practical value—the campaign gives simple, doable ideas for helping others. And, stories—every photo comes with a personal story behind it.
By weaving all these principles together, the campaign becomes more powerful than any single piece alone. Each part strengthens the others, creating a cycle where sharing and imitation just keep rolling.
But here’s something to keep in mind—not every idea needs to use all six principles in equal measure. The real trick is figuring out which levers fit your audience and context best, then designing your message or experience so those levers get pulled in just the right way.
So, how do you actually put this into practice? Start by taking a close look at your idea or product—are some principles already in play? What might be missing? Next, brainstorm ways to fill in the gaps. Can you make your idea more remarkable, more useful, or easier to spot?
Then, test it out. Watch how people react, and don’t be afraid to tweak things as you go. This isn’t a one-and-done process—it’s about experimenting and learning, discovering new ways to blend these principles for the biggest possible impact.
Ultimately, the goal is to create a cycle of sharing that feels natural and keeps going on its own—not just something that depends on paid ads or a stroke of luck.
